recent_candidates.excerpt: “Is this America's smartest—strangest—short-story writer?” —Leo Robson, The Telegraph I LIKED REX [https://www.nyrb.com/products/i-liked-rex]Diane Williams Diane Williams is one of the great masters of the American short story: her tiny, coruscating tales are among the most tender, funny, peculiar, and searching works in all of contemporary literature. I Liked Rex explores sex, love, marriage, and all that comes after; it is a book about living, but more importantly, about how to be alive. Williams's genius lies as much in what is left unspoken as in what is laid out on the page; behind images of startling beauty and strangeness, entire chamber dramas of the heart unfold, and the pleasure of these sphinxlike tales comes from their unremitting mystery, which is the same mystery fundamental to life and to love. recent_candidates.title: Blanchard’s Lathe and the Long Arc of American Manufacturing
recent_candidates.excerpt: Emerging from the chaos of supplying the U.S. Army during the War of 1812, the War Department sought to foster domestic production of standardized muskets. Out of this industrial project arose an invention that laid the foundation for automation and mass production. Thomas Blanchard’s copying lathe was a product of a fluid interchange between public and private interests, expertise, and capital. Born into the mechanical milieu of the nineteenth-century Connecticut River Valley, Blanchard embodied the period’s spirit of ingenuity. His creation enabled complex, irregular three-dimensional wood forms to be manufactured at scale. recent_candidates.title: Overcoming China’s Supply Chain Leverage
recent_candidates.excerpt: Since joining the World Trade Organization (WTO) in 2001, China has, barely without foreign notice, executed one of the most consequential economic strategies in modern history. When it entered the WTO, roughly 33 percent of Chinese exports were intermediate goods, or the components, chemicals, and parts that go into making final products. By 2025, that figure had risen to 46 percent.1 This did not happen by accident. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) made a deliberate strategic decision to, as it has framed it, make the world dependent on China while making China independent of the world.2 Supply chain supremacy was always intended as a geopolitical weapon. Continue reading Overcoming China’s Supply Chain Leverage on American Affairs Journal .

recent_candidates.title: Signs in the Furrows: Rural Resistance to the New Land Grab
recent_candidates.excerpt: A wiser national pattern would encourage states to default toward local control with guardrails, such as those outlined above, rather than broad preemption that severs decision-makers from consequences. Where states do retain override mechanisms, they should include strong prime farmland overlays, transparency mandates, and full accounting of long-term costs to neighboring properties and township budgets. This approach respects real infrastructure needs without repeating the moral failure of treating rural communities as blank slates for someone else’s metrics of progress. recent_candidates.title: Technology as Trojan Horse: The American Roots of European Erasure
recent_candidates.excerpt: America has its Promethean vision, which has undoubtedly served as a source of great wealth and vitality. Through technological deployment, however, it risks suffering the same fate as Icarus: burning its wings by seeking growth without meaning. Going higher and faster without knowing where you are going quickly becomes a nihilistic dead end that can lead to your own downfall. Europe still has its specific characteristics to counter this trend: ethical questions, a place given to humans that should not be the market’s adjustment variable, a greater role given to the collective over the individual compared to the American cultural paradigm. Continue reading Technology as Trojan Horse: The American Roots of European Erasure on American Affairs Journal .

recent_candidates.title: Unrest in the West: Anger and Aspiration in the Canadian Prairies
recent_candidates.excerpt: In October of 2026, Albertans will head to the polls for another referendum on a bundle of proposals that angle toward greater Albertan control over education, health care, the courts, and more power and leverage against the federal government. Five of ten questions relate to immigration restrictions, namely limiting access to public services and voting for noncitizens. But the referendum’s biggest bombshell is a question that reads: “Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?” In other words, Albertans are, for the first time in their history, being tested on whether they wish to secede entirely from Canada. And the question bites hard into a country already on edge about its sovereignty... Continue reading Unrest in the West: Anger and Aspiration in the Canadian Prairies on American Affairs Journal .

recent_candidates.title: Failing Like a State
recent_candidates.excerpt: Theories of technological domination are compelling not only because of their critical force but also because of their consolatory effect. They lend a certain heroism and grandeur to the idiocy and messiness of social decline. It is more honorable to imagine oneself as the victim of total surveillance and control than to admit that the disintegration of the social fabric and the deterioration of public discourse may arise from our own capacity for self-ruin. There is, in other words, something flattering about being oppressed. The fantasy of oppression spares us from confronting the fact that, compared to the history of democratic revolutions and liberation movements, our current predicament is a little embarrassing. The challenge of social criticism in the age of Big Tech may be to resist the allure of oppression narratives and develop ways of thinking through the strange banality of digital damage... Continue reading Failing Like a State on American Affairs Journal .

recent_candidates.title: The World That Never Was: Liberal Internationalism’s Last Crusade
recent_candidates.excerpt: In 1991, Michael McFaul felt that he was on the edge of utopia. Russia was free of communism, and America was free to usher in a new era of liberal internationalist hegemony. The arc of history had never bent so far toward justice. Over thirty years later, those dreams have crashed back to Earth. And in Autocrats vs. Democrats: China, Russia, America, and the New Global Disorder, McFaul seeks to put together how it all went wrong. His answer is unsurprising: an international movement of conservatives, led by Russian President Vladimir Putin, has sought to destroy democracy. With President Donald Trump’s election victories, they have nearly succeeded. Hope lies in a vigorous counterattack from the liberal internationalists. It would be very easy for conservatives and nationalists to dismiss his book as a musty last gasp of the post–Cold War liberal elite. His work might well be the literary equivalent of a Japanese soldier still fighting in 1975. But it should not be ignored... recent_candidates.title: The Augmentation-Automation Race
recent_candidates.excerpt: The actual effects of AI on the labor market still seem shrouded in deep uncertainty. When it comes to predictions on near-term impacts, we can see two camps emerge. A deep bench of established and renowned labor economists continues to expect “small” effect sizes, at least by the standards of the drastic predictions common in San Francisco. They predict local disruptions, yes, but expect they’ll be offset by broad-based productivity gains and job growth in other fields. Yet in much of Silicon Valley, a different view prevails. The creators of the technology, most prominently Anthropic’s CEO, Dario Amodei, predict widespread displacement and high unemployment. If there is absorption of the displaced, it will be into worse jobs that might not even be around for long. On that view, AI is markedly abnormal: while past technologies have complemented distinctly human contributions, such as intelligence or creativity, AI is sufficiently broad and general that we should expect it to exceed and supplant these human contributions to the economy, leaving human workers largely obsolete... Continue reading The Augmentation-Automation Race on American Affairs Journal .

recent_candidates.title: Don’t Wait for the Crisis: How Markets Can Fund National Resilience
recent_candidates.excerpt: The United States is rich in resources and poor in foresight. When Covid-19 arrived, the Strategic National Stockpile lacked a sufficient supply of N95 masks to equip the country’s critical workers through even a mild pandemic, let alone the reusable, pandemic-proof equipment that a more severe outbreak would demand. The available evidence suggests we are no better prepared today. This neglect exacerbates one of our greatest security vulnerabilities, as technology is only making it easier to engineer pandemics. But the same preparedness deficit recurs wherever critical goods are expensive to hold, seldom needed, and catastrophic to lack. The causes may seem obvious: markets underprovide public goods, and the state fails to fill the gap because policymakers are discouraged from investing in preparedness for events that probably won’t happen while they’re in office. Yet this clean story cannot explain why there are no private stockpiles contracted to supply private buyers... recent_candidates.title: The Debt-Equity Distinction: A Century of Policy by Accident
recent_candidates.excerpt: Our debt-heavy architecture is not a thought-out tenet of academic finance. Instead, it is substantially a function of practical circumstance: the deductibility of interest payments on corporate debt from pretax profits. That simple reality makes debt financing generally cheaper than raising equity. And while there are other reasons why businesses might want to use debt, especially the investment leverage that it provides to equity owners, the tax shield and the resulting lower “cost” of debt often tip the finance scales in favor of borrowing versus putting in one’s own capital. This bias was not part of the plan. Because there was no plan. Debt’s allure emerged not from careful deliberation about an optimal corporate capital structure at the University of Chicago, but from the exigencies of financing World War I. What began as a hastily adopted wartime measure has hardened through time to become a deeply rooted expectation. A century later, we inhabit a financial world substantially shaped by this distinction between cheaper debt and dearer equity. recent_candidates.title: Can America Build What It Cannot Insure?: Texas and California as Case Studies
recent_candidates.excerpt: The American housing debate still appears deceptively familiar: build more homes, loosen zoning restrictions, accelerate permitting, reduce construction costs, and help households qualify for mortgages. These goals remain important, especially in states where housing supply has failed to keep up with population and income growth. But they no longer fully capture what housing affordability now entails. A home must not only be permitted, built, purchased, and financed. It must also be insured. That requirement is becoming harder to satisfy. Homeowners insurance, once a routine escrow item, has become one of the main channels through which physical risk enters the household budget. Rising premiums arrive as higher monthly payments, wider deductibles, narrower coverage, nonrenewal notices, and new difficulties closing on a mortgage... recent_candidates.title: The Housing Divergence: Why Texas Builds and California Stalls
recent_candidates.excerpt: Americans have been voting with their feet and leaving California for Texas. There are many reasons for these moves, but foremost is that Texas has a lower cost of living, and by far the most important aspect of cost of living is housing. The obvious reason that California homes are more expensive is that the state makes it harder to build. But the question of why it is so much harder to build in California is not as obvious as some may think. In both Texas and California, land-use regulations are mainly local, and the states’ basic zoning-enabling laws for local government are similar... recent_candidates.title: The Prophets of Land: Texas, California, and the Coalitions That Rule Them
recent_candidates.excerpt: There is a temptation to categorize Texas and California under the two states’ traditional labels: Texas, the land of property rights; California, the land of regulation. But the truth is nearly the reverse. Texas does not actually hold that all property is sacred in the way property is commonly considered. It holds that the productive, extractive use of property outranks the passive holding of it. In California, a neighbor’s right to be heard can stop you from building on your own land; in Texas, a stranger’s right to use it can take it from you. As our legal academy is fond of pointing out, property is a bundle of rights, with none more impactful than possession and development. California has made the first sacred, Texas the second. But how did these two states develop such opposing systems of property rights? To answer that question requires winding back to the moment that both decided that they had had enough of that great American bogeyman, the railroad... Continue reading The Prophets of Land: Texas, California, and the Coalitions That Rule Them on American Affairs Journal .
